Lecture 40

Spherical separation and Legendre functions

Lecture objectives

We separate Laplace’s equation in spherical coordinates and prove that Legendre’s equation has a nonzero solution bounded on (−1,1)(-1,1)(−1,1) exactly when λ=ℓ(ℓ+1)\lambda=\ell(\ell+1)λ=ℓ(ℓ+1) with an integer ℓ≥0.\ell\ge0ℓ≥0. We derive Rodrigues’ formula and the norms of the Legendre polynomials, prove their completeness from polynomial approximation, and expand an axisymmetric potential inside and outside a sphere.

Lecture 39 separated the Laplacian in a disc and found a radial problem with one singular endpoint. A sphere leads, after separation in spherical coordinates, to Legendre’s equation on (−1,1),(-1,1)(−1,1), whose coefficient p(x)=1−x2p(x)=1-x^2p(x)=1−x2 vanishes at both ends. In this lecture we decide which solutions are admissible there, construct the Legendre polynomials, prove that they are complete, and use them to find the potential inside and outside a sphere with given boundary values. The lecture reads in three stages: separation and the singular angular problem (Sections 40.1 and 40.2), the Legendre polynomials and their completeness (Sections 40.3 and 40.4), and potentials of a sphere (Section 40.5).

We consider real λ,\lambdaλ, the values that a separation of real fields produces.

Definition 40.1 (Legendre’s eigenvalue problem). A real number λ\lambdaλ is an eigenvalue of Legendre’s problem if (40.2) has a solution y∈C2(−1,1),y\in C^2(-1,1)y∈C2(−1,1), not identically zero, that is bounded on (−1,1).(-1,1)(−1,1). Such a yyy is an eigenfunction for λ.\lambdaλ.

Theorem 40.2 (Eigenvalues of Legendre’s problem). For Legendre’s problem the following hold.

  • Integer modes. The eigenvalues of Legendre’s problem are the numbers λ=ℓ(ℓ+1)\lambda=\ell(\ell+1)λ=ℓ(ℓ+1) with ℓ∈{0,1,2,…}.\ell\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}ℓ∈{0,1,2,…}.

  • Polynomial eigenfunctions. For λ=ℓ(ℓ+1)\lambda=\ell(\ell+1)λ=ℓ(ℓ+1) the eigenfunctions are the nonzero multiples of one polynomial of degree ℓ,\ellℓ, which is even or odd as ℓ\ellℓ is. So every eigenvalue is simple.

  • Orthogonality. Eigenfunctions yyy and zzz for different eigenvalues satisfy ∫−11y(x)z(x) ⁣dx=0.\int_{-1}^1y(x)z(x)\dd x=0∫−11​y(x)z(x)dx=0.

The other two, sin⁡θcos⁡φ\sin\theta\cos\varphisinθcosφ and sin⁡θsin⁡φ,\sin\theta\sin\varphisinθsinφ, carry the azimuthal pair cos⁡φ\cos\varphicosφ and sin⁡φ,\sin\varphisinφ, Lecture 36’s periodic example of an eigenvalue that is not simple.

40.3 Legendre polynomials

40.4 Completeness of the Legendre polynomials

Summary

Separating Laplace’s equation in spherical coordinates gives the radial powers rℓr^\ellrℓ and r−ℓ−1r^{-\ell-1}r−ℓ−1 and, for axisymmetric fields, Legendre’s equation −((1−x2)y′)′=λy-((1-x^2)y')'=\lambda y−((1−x2)y′)′=λy with x=cos⁡θ.x=\cos\thetax=cosθ. Both ends x=±1x=\pm1x=±1 are singular. Boundedness there forces λ=ℓ(ℓ+1)\lambda=\ell(\ell+1)λ=ℓ(ℓ+1) and selects the polynomial solution Pℓ.P_\ellPℓ​. For two polynomial solutions the end terms of the boundary form tend to 0.00. For an unbounded solution they need not, and orthogonality can fail: ∫−11xartanh⁡x ⁣dx=1.\int_{-1}^1x\operatorname{artanh}x\dd x=1∫−11​xartanhxdx=1. The Legendre polynomials are orthogonal and complete, and they expand the boundary values of an axisymmetric potential of a sphere.

  • Integer modes: a nonzero solution of Legendre’s equation bounded on (−1,1)(-1,1)(−1,1) exists exactly for λ=ℓ(ℓ+1),\lambda=\ell(\ell+1)λ=ℓ(ℓ+1), ℓ∈{0,1,2,…},\ell\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}ℓ∈{0,1,2,…}, and is a multiple of Pℓ.P_\ellPℓ​.

  • Rodrigues: Pℓ=12ℓℓ! ⁣dℓ ⁣dxℓ(x2−1)ℓ,P_\ell=\frac1{2^\ell\ell!}\frac{\dd^\ell}{\dd x^\ell}(x^2-1)^\ellPℓ​=2ℓℓ!1​dxℓdℓ​(x2−1)ℓ, Pℓ(1)=1,P_\ell(1)=1Pℓ​(1)=1, Pℓ(−x)=(−1)ℓPℓ(x),P_\ell(-x)=(-1)^\ell P_\ell(x)Pℓ​(−x)=(−1)ℓPℓ​(x), ∣Pℓ∣≤1\abs{P_\ell}\le1∣Pℓ​∣≤1 on [−1,1].[-1,1][−1,1].

Self-check

4 questions. Answer without looking back at the notes; a first miss gives a hint and a second try. Enter numbers with a decimal point.

1. For an axisymmetric harmonic field, the polar factor is the degree-two Legendre polynomial, so the radial equation is (r2R′)′=6R(r^2R')'=6R(r2R′)′=6R. Which radial powers are admissible inside a sphere with a bounded centre and outside it with decay at infinity, respectively?

Hint. Substitute a power of rrr into the radial equation, then test the two roots at opposite ends of the radial range.

For R=rsR=r^sR=rs the equation becomes s(s+1)=6s(s+1)=6s(s+1)=6. The roots are 222 and −3-3−3. The power r2r^2r2 stays bounded at the centre and grows at infinity, while r−3r^{-3}r−3 diverges at the centre and decays at infinity. The pair with exponent −2-2−2 misses the extra unit in the negative root. The pair with exponents 333 and −4-4−4 solves the radial equation for the next degree.

2. On −1<x<1-1<x<1−1<x<1, the axisymmetric angular equation is ((1−x2)y′)′+λy=0((1-x^2)y')'+\lambda y=0((1−x2)y′)′+λy=0. What selects the admissible values of λ\lambdaλ for a nonzero solution on a sphere?

Hint. The endpoints correspond to the poles of the sphere. Recall what happens to an ordinary-point series that does not terminate.

The physical requirement is boundedness at both poles. Taking the even and odd parts preserves that boundedness. The lecture’s recurrence forces a nonterminating part to diverge as x→1−x\to1^-x→1−. A nonzero bounded part therefore terminates, giving a Legendre polynomial and λ=ℓ(ℓ+1)\lambda=\ell(\ell+1)λ=ℓ(ℓ+1) for a nonnegative integer ℓ\ellℓ. The bounded polynomial also has (1−x2)y′→0(1-x^2)y'\to0(1−x2)y′→0 at each end. These endpoints are singular, so the regular separated theorem does not select them. Zero values at both poles are not imposed, and analyticity only in the open interval holds even for solutions that diverge at the poles.

3. On [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1], expand f(x)=x2f(x)=x^2f(x)=x2 in Legendre polynomials normalized by Pℓ(1)=1P_\ell(1)=1Pℓ​(1)=1. Find the coefficient of P2P_2P2​ and round to two decimal places.

Enter a valid number using a decimal point.

Hint. Use Rodrigues’ formula for the degree-two polynomial and project with unit weight.

Rodrigues’ formula gives P2(x)=18 ⁣d2 ⁣dx2(x2−1)2=(3x2−1)/2P_2(x)=\frac18\frac{\dd^2}{\dd x^2}(x^2-1)^2=(3x^2-1)/2P2​(x)=81​dx2d2​(x2−1)2=(3x2−1)/2. Then x2=1/3+(2/3)P2(x)x^2=1/3+(2/3)P_2(x)x2=1/3+(2/3)P2​(x). The constant is a multiple of P0P_0P0​ and is orthogonal to P2P_2P2​, so the coefficient is 2/32/32/3, or 0.67 to two decimal places. The leading coefficient 3/23/23/2 of the polynomial must be inverted to match the leading term of x2x^2x2.

4. A sphere of radius aaa has axisymmetric, piecewise continuous prescribed values f(x)f(x)f(x) with x=cos⁡θx=\cos\thetax=cosθ. The profile has a jump. In what sense does the bounded interior Legendre potential take these boundary values as r→a−r\to a^-r→a−?

Hint. Consider the norm used for Legendre completeness. The radial factors tend to one for each fixed mode.

For the interior solution the mode factor is (r/a)ℓ(r/a)^\ell(r/a)ℓ. As r→a−r\to a^-r→a− it tends to one for each ℓ\ellℓ and has magnitude at most one. Parseval’s identity bounds the squared norm of the difference by a summable series of squared coefficients with their Legendre norms. Passing to the limit gives mean-square convergence with measure  ⁣dx\dd xdx. At fixed interior radii the profiles are continuous, so the jump rules out uniform boundary convergence. The theorem does not assert a pointwise value at the jump. The squared norm also cannot be tested only at the polar axis.
